title: Dashoguz buyers seek reversal of a cotton-oil ration cut
participants_original: The report describes numerous buyer complaints, demands, and threats but gives no participant count.
threshold_50_evidence: Not established. “Numerous” does not demonstrate at least 50 people; the number of ration recipients is not turnout.

title.summary: The article reports buyer demands after a regulated cotton-oil allocation was reduced at Shop No. 32.

start_date.summary: The report states the ration cut occurred on 11 January and describes buyer complaints and demands in the same account; it does not give the time or duration of the collective action.

end_date.summary: No physical departure, dissolution, or end time is reported; the quota reversal is not treated as the physical end.

location.summary: The report identifies Shop No. 32 in Dashoguz.

scope.summary: The account concerns a single store in Dashoguz; no wider multi-site action is described.

organizer.summary: The article refers to buyers/customers and names no organizer.

demands.summary: Buyers demanded reversal of the reduced cotton-oil allocation. The available seven demand categories do not clearly represent this specific quantity/ration issue, so none is assigned.

participants_original.summary: The source says numerous buyer complaints/demands but gives no attendance number.

participants_min.summary: No numerical lower bound for people taking part in a public action is reported.

participants_max.summary: No numerical upper bound is reported.

threshold_50_evidence.summary: “Numerous” is not a numerical or clear qualitative estimate of 50 or more; ration recipients or customers cannot be converted to turnout.

protester_violence.summary: The report mentions threats to damage the shop but does not report physical violence by participants; code remains unknown.

state_response.summary: Accommodation=yes: the article says the allowance returned to its former level after buyer complaints and demands. It does not identify who ordered the restoration. No arrests, beatings, dispersal, explicit ignoring, killings, or shootings are reported, so those dimensions remain unknown.

eligibility.summary: The source documents buyer demands over a state-regulated ration and an apparent response, but does not establish a count of 50 or one identifiable public gathering; retained pending evidence.

notes: This is a tentative local buyer-action lead, not an approved protest record. The article documents a ration cut and reversal but does not establish how many people acted together or whether complaints were made in one public gathering. Keep separate from the 16 January queue in Sayat district/Lebap; shared food-supply concerns do not establish one episode.
open_questions: Was there one public gathering at Shop No. 32, and how many people participated?
Who ordered the ration reversal, and was the cut a state policy or a store-level decision?
What were the action's physical start and end beyond the reported 11 January sequence?
Can an independent contemporaneous outlet corroborate the event and turnout?

title: Buyers object to reduced subsidized oil rations at a Lebap village shop
location: Agricultural Association Azatlyk state shop, Sayat district, Lebap province; the shop served Gyzan, Alpan, and Araptelman villages
participants_original: The source describes people queueing and beginning to object after a ration reduction; it gives no number of shoppers or demonstrators.
threshold_50_evidence: Not established. A queue serving three villages and the phrase “people began to object” do not quantify attendance or establish at least 50 participants.

title.summary: The second article also describes objections after the reduced cotton-oil ration was announced; it explicitly attributes the account to Chronicles of Turkmenistan.

start_date.summary: The second article confirms the queue at the Sayat state shop on 16 January and says people began lining up at 4 a.m.; it explicitly identifies Chronicles of Turkmenistan as its source.

end_date.summary: No departure, dissolution, or physical end of the queue/action is reported; scheduled sales through 18 January do not establish that the same gathering continued.

location.summary: The second article identifies the same Agricultural Association Azatlyk state shop in Sayat district and the three villages it served; it attributes the reporting to Chronicles, so this is not independent location corroboration.

scope.summary: Only one shop and its queue are described; the three villages are its service area, not three protest sites.

organizer.summary: The source describes shoppers in a queue and names no organizer.

demands.summary: The second article repeats that the shop reduced the cotton-oil ration and changed which village could buy on which day; the woman objected to the late notice. It cites Chronicles and does not add an independent state-policy demand.

participants_original.summary: The article reports people queueing and says the people in line began to object; no attendance number is given.

participants_min.summary: The article does not establish a numerical minimum of people participating in protest activity; queue size is not given.

participants_max.summary: No maximum or total queue size is reported.

threshold_50_evidence.summary: The queue served three villages, but the number present or protesting is not stated; service area and ration recipients are not attendance.

protester_violence.summary: The account reports verbal objections and shouting, not physical violence by protesters; no-explicit is not justified from this limited account, so unknown is retained.

state_response.summary: The second article repeats the report that the seller called police and the 56-year-old woman was taken to the Sayat police department, explicitly citing Chronicles. This is the same reporting chain, not independent corroboration; other response dimensions remain unknown.

eligibility.summary: Turkmen.News repeats the Chronicles account of the queue and individual objection, but does not add an attendance count and is not an independent source. Threshold and whether this was a protest rather than a queue dispute remain unresolved.

notes: Do not treat the queue as a known 50-person gathering. The report's photograph caption describes an Ashgabat food queue from October 2020, not evidence about this January event. The article also mentions a separate 11 January Dashoguz shop action, which is not merged here.
open_questions: How many people were in the queue and how many actively objected?
Was the queue gathering an identifiable public protest, or a routine food line with an individual complaint?
What was the physical end of the queue/action?
Did any state official or shop manager address the demand apart from closing the shop and calling police?
Can an independent contemporaneous source corroborate the reported arrest/detention and chronology?

title: Job seekers resist police dispersal at the Gulanly stop near Shatlyk
location: Gulanly bus stop beside a fuel station on the outskirts of Shatlyk, Mary region
participants_original: Radio Azatlyk reports more than 50 people; CABAR summarizes the number as about 50. Fergana and the Labor Mission repeat the report, with both explicitly attributing it to Azatlyk.
threshold_50_evidence: Reported estimates sit around the threshold: Azatlyk says more than 50, while CABAR says about 50; Fergana and Labor Mission explicitly repeat Azatlyk. There is no exact or independent count, so turnout reliability remains unresolved. January ownership is separately pending because the physical date is unknown.

title.summary: The reports describe job seekers resisting police demands to leave while trying to travel from Shatlyk to Ashgabat for work. The Labor Mission body also identifies the action as disobedience over travel restrictions and explicitly attributes the report to Azatlyk.

start_date.summary: CABAR places the item in a January 2021 review, Azatlyk published on 13 January, and Fergana on 14 January. The Labor Mission body says Azatlyk reported it on 14 January but gives no gathering date. Azatlyk quotes a correspondent reporting on 12 August without a year; Fergana and Labor Mission do not establish the physical date. Physical month ownership remains unresolved, so start_date is null.

end_date.summary: The report says people were transported to the police station, released with warnings, and moved 500 metres away; it does not establish when the gathering physically ended or whether the relocated group continued.

location.summary: CABAR, Azatlyk, Fergana, and the Labor Mission body identify the Gulanly stop near a fuel station on the outskirts of Shatlyk, Mary region; the latter two explicitly derive the report from Azatlyk.

scope.summary: The reports concern one local bus stop; the Labor Mission page adds no other sites.

organizer.summary: Sources identify local residents/job seekers and no organizer; the Labor Mission report does not name one.

demands.summary: Residents sought travel to Ashgabat for jobs amid restrictions on interregional movement. The Labor Mission body explicitly attributes the account to Azatlyk. The seven demand categories do not clearly represent access to work/internal travel, so none is assigned.

participants_original.summary: Azatlyk says more than 50, CABAR says about 50, Fergana's headline says about 50, and the Labor Mission body repeats “more than 50” while explicitly citing Azatlyk. The latter repetitions are not independent counts.

participants_min.summary: No reliable numeric lower bound is established. Azatlyk reports more than 50, CABAR says about 50, and Fergana/Labor Mission repeat the Azatlyk account; the latter two are not independent counts. Keep participants_min null and attendance uncertain.

participants_max.summary: No upper bound or exact attendance count is reported.

threshold_50_evidence.summary: Reported estimates sit around the threshold: Azatlyk says more than 50, while CABAR says about 50; Fergana and Labor Mission explicitly repeat Azatlyk. There is no exact or independent count, so turnout reliability remains unresolved. January ownership is separately pending because the physical date is unknown.

protester_violence.summary: The account reports refusal to comply with police orders but no physical violence by protesters; limited reporting leaves violence unknown.

state_response.summary: Azatlyk, Fergana, and the Labor Mission body report that police demanded the group disperse/leave and then transported people to a police station; Fergana and the Labor Mission explicitly attribute their account to Azatlyk. Code crowd_dispersal=yes for the attributed dispersal attempt and arrests=yes for being taken to the station. No other response dimensions are established.

eligibility.summary: A public group of job seekers, attempted police dispersal, transport to a station, and an employment/travel grievance are reported. Estimates are around 50 and may derive from Azatlyk; the additional Fergana and Labor Mission pages explicitly cite Azatlyk. Turnout remains uncertain, and the physical-date conflict prevents January assignment (pending_unit).

notes: Do not assign this event to January 2021 yet. CABAR includes the story in its January review; Azatlyk published on 13 January, and Fergana and the Labor Mission article appeared in the January reporting chain, but Azatlyk's text quotes a correspondent reporting “12 August,” without a year. Fergana and the Labor Mission do not resolve the physical date and both explicitly attribute the report to Azatlyk. The web open for the Labor Mission page returned Cache miss; default DNS failed on the exact URL, then one authorized ordinary HTTPS GET returned HTTP 200 at the same URL and the body still did not state the event date. Keep physical date and unit ownership unresolved.
open_questions: Does any contemporaneous source establish whether “12 August” was 2020 or whether the gathering occurred in January 2021?
Why do January publication/report dates coexist with the August correspondent report date?
Is any evidence independent of Azatlyk? Fergana and the Labor Mission page explicitly cite Azatlyk; CABAR's exact reporting chain remains to be established.
What was the physical end after people were taken to the station?
Can the reported restriction be tied to a state policy or decision-maker and mapped to an original demand category?

title: Food queues at Bayramali state shops face police dispersal
location: State food shops in Bayramali, Mary region; exact stores not identified
participants_original: The article describes huge crowds at state shops but gives no numerical attendance count.
threshold_50_evidence: Not established. The source's phrase “huge crowds” supplies no explicit number or hundreds/thousands estimate.

title.summary: The article reports that police tried to disperse early-morning food queues at state shops in Bayramali; residents shouted back and said they were there to get bread.

start_date.summary: S037 dates its first-hand queue observation to 8 January and says police appeared daily. S038 reports Bayramali queues on 5 and 6 January, but does not establish the same people or episode; it cannot date E005’s physical onset. Keep start_date null.

end_date.summary: The article describes a recurring daily queue and no departure/dissolution or physical end for the observed group.

location.summary: The title says Mary, while the article body identifies the observed queues at state stores in Bayramali, Mary region; it gives no exact store.

scope.summary: The report identifies queues at state stores in Bayramali; no other city or region is described.

organizer.summary: No organizer is named in the limited body extraction.

demands.summary: People said they were standing for bread and had little hope of buying other food. The source does not establish an explicit policy demand or a demand directed to a state decision-maker; no category is assigned.

participants_original.summary: The body calls the queues huge crowds but provides no exact count.

participants_min.summary: No numerical lower bound appears in the body extraction.

participants_max.summary: No numerical upper bound appears in the body extraction.

threshold_50_evidence.summary: The phrase “huge crowds” is qualitative but not a supported numerical estimate of at least 50 or of hundreds/thousands; threshold remains unknown.

protester_violence.summary: The selected body passages describe verbal replies to police but no physical violence; limited page read leaves the dimension unknown.

state_response.summary: Crowd_dispersal=yes: the title and body say police vehicles arrived and officials attempted to disperse queues. The selected body passages do not establish arrests, beatings, accommodation, explicit ignoring, killings, or shootings; those remain unknown.

eligibility.summary: S037 describes a public queue, verbal resistance to attempted police dispersal, and bread scarcity but does not establish a protest demand or threshold. S038 reports earlier queues at Bayramali but no protest, explicit demand, police contact, or link to the 8 January observation; its queue-size wording is not protest turnout. Retain pending_evidence.

notes: Azattyq Asia's 9 January article attributes the first-hand observation to a Radio Azatlyk correspondent on 8 January. It describes police appearing at state shops every day to disperse early-morning queues in Bayramali and a verbal exchange about standing for bread. The repeated daily pattern's physical start/end is unknown, and the written byline/republication relationship was not captured. It remains a lead, not a qualifying protest determination. S038 additionally describes Bayramali queues on 5 and 6 January, but does not establish they involved the same people or episode as the 8 January observation, an explicit protest demand, or police dispersal. Its text credits Radio Azatlyk correspondents; the written byline/republication relation is not captured, so it is not independent confirmation of E005. The reported queue size is not protest turnout.
open_questions: Was the observed food queue a deliberate protest or an ordinary line with verbal responses to police?
How many people were present or actively resisting?
When did the recurring daily queue/police interaction begin and end?
Was there an explicit demand addressed to the state, beyond standing for bread?
Does the written reporting originate with Radio Azatlyk or Azattyq Asia?
